newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Russia, Ukraine seal delayed friendship treaty.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Ukraine seal delayed friendship treaty.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma ended years of acrimony between the two Slav states on Saturday by signing a friendship treaty and shaping long-term economic and political cooperation.

They signed a treaty on a "strategic partnership" and another three documents including a broad political declaration on bilateral and international problems, statements on the Black Sea Fleet and cooperation on economic issues and in space.

Both leaders have said the summit meeting, postponed at least six times, had become possible after lengthy talks between Kuchma and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Wednesday when they agreed terms for Moscow to keep its share of the fleet at Ukraine's Sevastopol port.
Yeltsin, vigorous and in upbeat mood, told war veterans as he paid tribute to victims of World War Two at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier: "We cannot live without each other.
"We respect and honour the territorial integrity of Ukraine," Yeltsin added.

Russian parliamentarians have urged the Kremlin to claim Sevastopol on the Crimean peninsula, base of the disputed Black Sea Fleet, which was ceded to Soviet Ukraine from Russia by Nikita Khrushchev in a largely symbolic gesture in 1954.
But Yeltsin made his opposition to parliament clear and warned his colleagues in Moscow that they better take relations with Ukraine seriously -- or else.
"My friend President Kuchma and I, at this sacred place, at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, swear that the agreement we sign today will be fulfilled," Yeltsin said.
"I will tell ministers in Moscow: 'Just try forgetting that Ukraine is the priority of all priorities and you'll have the president to deal with," Yeltsin declared.

Yeltsin has signed five deals with Ukraine regarding the fleet since Kiev broke ties with Moscow, taking Sevastopol and the became part of its territory but none of the agreements solved the problem in the long term.

Moscow and Kiev have said they are keen to end their squabbles over the Soviet heritage and dramatically improve long-term relations between the two Slav pillars of the Commonwealth of Independent States.
